job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: David Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thank you for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I cycle to a shared office in Manchester's Northern Quarter, where I'm a junior backend developer at a small company that makes appointment software for GPs' surgeries. Mornings are stand-up and bug tickets, afternoons are writing small features with a more senior colleague, Priya, reviewing my code. I started in September after a degree in software engineering at Salford.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the moment a bug finally makes sense, and I like that our software helps surgeries send fewer people home without an appointment. The tiring part is that the company is small and funding is tight, so everyone watches the cash. I share a house with two friends, Tom and Jas, and my dad's taxi firm is the family backstop if I ever need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's useful but overhyped. I use the coding assistant a bit, and it saves me maybe an hour a day on boring bits. A coding assistant helps me write code faster, but it doesn't tell me what the surgery actually needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm a bit uneasy, but for a different reason: our company's money. We have about a year of runway, and the boss keeps mentioning a funding round. If that falls through, AI isn't what takes my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, build my skills on the backend side and take the testing training our company offers. I'd put 300 pounds a month into savings and my pension. I'd keep a CV ready, just in case the startup wobbles.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly okay, but with a small knot about the company. It's the ordinary startup knot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the funding is tight. What does that look like day to day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've stopped buying the nice coffee, which sounds silly, but it's how you know. Our boss, Marcus, holds a monthly all-hands now and talks about runway in months. We're fine, but you can feel it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your dad, who runs the taxi firm, about all this hype?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to keep an eye on the self-driving talk, but not to panic. He says taxis will always need a human who knows the streets. I tell him that's what every industry says, then I feel bad.

say: I'd say AI is **useful but overhyped**; it saves me an hour a day.
I'd tell friends my real worry is company **funding**, not AI.
think: I'm slightly **uneasy**, because the startup has about a year of runway.
If the funding round fails, AI isn't what takes my job.
do: Build my **backend** skills and take the testing training the firm offers.
Put **300 pounds** a month into savings and my pension.
Keep my **CV** ready in case the startup wobbles.
feel: Fairly okay, with a small **knot** about the company's money.
S0.quote: A coding assistant helps me write code faster, but it doesn't tell me what the surgery actually needs.
fieldNote: His worry is the **startup's cash**, not AI; the plateau changes nothing there.
He uses the coding assistant in a measured way.
Family backstop (his father's firm) is real but he'd rather not use it.

steps.text: Take the company's testing training and ask Priya to review harder tickets
Use the coding assistant for test writing only
Put 300 pounds a month into savings and the pension

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real now, not hype. At the office I'd argue we should use it carefully and train juniors on review and testing. Anyone who writes code for a living should assume half of it will soon be written by a machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm anxious. Junior work is exactly what the assistants do well: small features, tests, boring fixes. My company may think two seniors with the tools can do what three of us did, and I'm the third.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the tools properly rather than occasionally, and take a cloud and security course, because those need judgement. I'd ask Marcus for review and design tasks. I'd also join a tech workers' union group, because I think we should have a voice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but also curious. I've got savings, so I'm not drowning, but I can see the ground moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your work would software take first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing the first version of anything: forms, tests, simple screens. I already let the assistant do most of those, and I check them. The part I keep is deciding what to build and spotting what's wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you think happens to juniors at a place like yours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They stop being hired, mostly. A senior plus a good assistant looks cheaper than a senior plus a junior who needs two years. I hope Priya fights for me, but she has her own targets.

say: I'd say the change is **real now** and juniors should train on review and testing.
I'd argue firms must not treat people as the **cheap** part of the tool.
think: I'm **anxious**, because junior work is what the assistants do best.
My firm may decide two seniors plus tools can replace three of us.
do: Learn the tools **properly**, not occasionally, and take a cloud and security course.
Ask Marcus for **review** and design tasks.
feel: **Anxious** but curious, since I can see the ground moving.
S1.quote: Anyone who writes code for a living should assume half of it will soon be written by a machine.
fieldNote: He treats review and **judgement** as the escape from junior work.
He is fair to his colleague Priya and does not blame her.
Union interest comes from fairness, not from anger.

steps.text: Use the coding assistant daily for first drafts and check every line
Take a cloud security course in the evenings
Join the tech workers' union group in Manchester

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need rules and a safety net now, and I'd say it publicly. Online I'd back calls for a shorter week and a public retraining fund. Two years is no time at all to rebuild an economy that took two hundred years to build.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be scared, to be honest. Coding is the exact thing they list first, and I'm at the bottom of the ladder. I'd expect junior developers to be gone from most companies within about a year of AGI, and my boss to be telling us it's nothing personal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut every non-essential cost, stop going out, and double my savings rate. I'd talk to my parents about whether I could move into the room above the taxi office for a while. I'd learn plumbing basics with my uncle, honestly, because robots with hands are three years behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I think I'd lose my job, and it's keeping me up even now. It's the speed that kills me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only two years, how would you think about your savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd count how many months I can last: about seven with my savings, longer if I move home. I'd stop paying for anything I can't cancel quickly, and I'd keep the money in a boring account. I wouldn't gamble on shares, because I might need it all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tom and Jas, your housemates?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them over a curry that I might have to move out. Tom works in a bank and Jas is a nurse. I think Jas would be fine, and Tom would be as worried as me.

say: I'd back a **shorter week** and a public retraining fund, loudly.
I'd say two years is too short for the economy to **adapt**.
think: I'd be **scared**, since coding is the first thing on the AGI list.
I expect junior developers to be gone within about a year of **AGI**.
do: Cut non-essential costs and **double** my savings rate.
Ask my parents about living above the **taxi office** for a while.
Learn **plumbing** basics with my uncle, because robots for hands come later.
feel: **Alarmed**, and the speed is what frightens me.
S2.quote: Two years is no time at all to rebuild an economy that took two hundred years to build.
fieldNote: He expects to lose the job, which fits **alarmed** despite savings.
The plumbing idea is serious but half a joke; he keeps it as a hedge.
He values family backing and says he'd use it only if forced.

steps.text: Cancel every subscription and stop eating out
Keep seven months of savings in a plain account
Ask my parents about moving above the taxi office
Spend Saturdays learning plumbing basics with my uncle

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's frightening but five years gives us a fighting chance. I'd push for unions and governments to agree retraining before it starts. Five years is long enough to learn a trade and short enough that you can't put it off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious, but I feel I have some control. If I use the time well I could shift into something where a human is still required: cyber security, medical software with rules, or running AI systems. That's still thinking work, though, so I'm not fully sure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the firm for two years and learn everything about health data and regulation, because the law will make us keep humans in the loop. I'd save 500 pounds a month. Then I'd study for a security qualification in the evenings and maybe a part-time master's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, not terrified. Five years feels like the first level where I can plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the extra three years before robots reach hands-on work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at jobs where someone has to take responsibility: medical software, safety, audits. The extra robot years suggest hands-on trades, but I'm a keyboard person. I could imagine running a small team that checks the machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay in software at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might, but with a different job description. I'd keep writing code a bit, because I like it, even if it's no longer my main income.

say: I'd say five years is a **fighting chance** if unions and governments plan retraining.
I'd push for retraining **before** the change starts.
think: I'm anxious but have some **control** if I use the time well.
Even security or audit work is **thinking** work, so I'm not sure.
do: Stay at the firm and learn health **data** and regulation.
Save **500 pounds** a month and study security in the evenings.
Consider a part-time **master's** in the second year.
feel: **Worried**, not terrified, because five years is a length I can plan.
S3.quote: Five years is long enough to learn a trade and short enough that you can't put it off.
fieldNote: He chooses regulated, **responsibility** jobs as his shelter, and admits the doubt.
The extra robot years do not tempt him: he calls himself a keyboard person.
Savings rate rises but he avoids panic moves.

steps.text: Stay at the company and learn health data law
Study for a security qualification in the evenings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a lot of time and people should use it well. Online I'd support a public retraining fund and a four-day week. Ten years is enough to retrain twice, if the government pays for the first time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm fairly calm, because by then I'd be 32 and could have a second profession. I'd still be a bit uneasy about what the world looks like, but it's not about my job. I'd want to be in a role that guides the machines or a role that serves people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the job and build the skills I enjoy. I'd save toward a deposit on a flat, do a part-time master's in data or health informatics, and use the AI tools more every year. I'd also do some volunteering with a digital skills charity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, with some curiosity. Ten years feels like a normal career, with one big uncertain bend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently if you knew the date was 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably nothing dramatic. I'd put a bit more into learning the tools, since by then everyone will. I'd choose a masters in health informatics, because healthcare will still need people in the loop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about starting a family, or buying a place?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still plan for them, but with care. A flat in ten years, children maybe, and a job that doesn't depend on one skill. The date doesn't change my love life, but it changes my mortgage choices.

say: I'd say ten years is a lot and a **public retraining fund** should use it.
think: I'm fairly **calm**, since by 32 I could have a second profession.
I'd want a role that guides the machines or serves **people**.
do: Save toward a **deposit** on a flat and keep my current job.
Do a part-time **master's** in health informatics.
feel: **Calm**, with some curiosity about the big uncertain bend.
S4.quote: Ten years is enough to retrain twice, if the government pays for the first time.
fieldNote: Ten years lets him treat AGI as a **career bend**, not a cliff.
He links his plans to health informatics, the field his company serves.
Mild unease remains about society, not his own job.

steps.text: Save toward a flat deposit while renting with housemates
Start a part-time master's in health informatics
Use the AI tools more each year at work
Plan a flat and children for my early thirties

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Two years, definitely. I've got savings and a family firm to fall back on, and still the only plan I have is not to panic. Help would be a public retraining fund, a shorter working week and companies being made to say honestly what they're cutting.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Just that nobody asked my generation if we wanted this. My dad's drivers say the same thing about taxis and self-driving cars. I'd like people who do the work to sit in the room.

headlineQuote: I've got savings and a family firm to fall back on, and still the only plan I have is not to panic.
portrait: David is **22**, a software engineering graduate working as a junior backend developer at a small Manchester health-software company.
He has no debt, over six months saved and a father with a taxi firm as a family backstop.
He is progressive, blames **big firms** and shareholders for the speed, and likes unions and public retraining.
He is steady: he uses AI tools and moves once something is proven, but expects junior coders to go first.
biggestWorry: AI by **2028** worries him most, because junior coding is the first work it takes.
whatWouldHelp: A **public retraining fund**, a shorter working week and honest disclosure of cuts by companies.
